quote: Giebt es im $R_3$ Flächen, singularitätenfrei, die nur eine geschlossene Selbstdurchdringungskurve mit einem 6 fachen oder 2 dreifachen [-...-] Doppelpunkt hat?
english: Are there singularity-free surfaces in $R_3$ that have only one closed self-intersection curve with one sixfold double point or two threefold double points?
topic: Notes on: a physics question about why motion becomes critical at the speed of sound or light; eigenfunction expansions in the calculus of variations; questions about analogues and properties of Boy's surface; and a plan to extend Darboux's conformal mapping theory from cyclic quartics to cyclic curves of sixth order.

triage.modern_statement: This looks like a follow-up to Boy's surface. Boy's surface is an immersion of the real projective plane RP^2 in R^3 whose only self-intersection is one closed double-point curve, and that curve meets itself at a single triple point. A modern reading of Hilbert's question: is there a closed surface, generically immersed in R^3 with no singularities other than self-intersections, whose double-point set is one connected closed curve and whose only higher-multiplicity points are either (a) a single point where the double curve passes through itself several times (Hilbert's '6-fach', which I read as a point of higher multiplicity than a triple point, though the exact meaning is unclear; it would be a non-generic singularity), or (b) exactly two triple points? Hilbert does not say which surface or topological type he means. The illegible bracketed word in the transcription adds more uncertainty.
triage.answered_by: I found no source that answers Hilbert's question in this exact form. The closest later result is Thomas F. Banchoff, 'Triple points and surgery of immersed surfaces', Proc. AMS, March 1974. It shows that for a generic immersion of a closed surface in E^3, the number of triple points has the same parity (even or odd) as the surface's Euler characteristic. So a surface with exactly two triple points must have even Euler characteristic, for example a sphere, torus or Klein bottle, and cannot be the projective plane. Immersed spheres with exactly two triple points do exist; one is 'Banchoff's sphere', studied for example in arXiv:1707.02823. But I could not confirm from sources that any such example has a single connected double curve.

evidence.claim: Boy's surface is a map of the real projective plane into R^3 with one continuous double-point curve that meets itself in a triple point; these are its only self-intersections.
Boy's surface is one of the two possible immersions of the real projective plane that have only a single triple point.
Banchoff: for a generic immersion of a closed surface into E^3, the number of triple points is congruent mod 2 to the Euler characteristic.
Banchoff's paper 'Triple Points and Surgery of Immersed Surfaces' is dated March 1974, and generalizations of his triple point theorem were published later.
'Banchoff's sphere' is a known immersed sphere with only two triple points. It is described as one of the three unique filling Dehn spheres of S^3 with only two triple points.

triage.why: This is a genuine but loosely stated question about the self-intersection structure of immersed surfaces, prompted by Boy's surface. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem, and I found no source that cites or answers it directly. Later theory does constrain it: Banchoff's 1974 parity theorem rules out two triple points on the projective plane, and examples with two triple points exist, such as Banchoff's sphere. Research on the self-intersections of immersed surfaces, such as triple point counts and filling Dehn spheres, continues today. However, I could not confirm whether anyone has shown a surface whose double curve is one closed curve with exactly two triple points. I also cannot pin down what Hilbert meant by the '6-fach' case, and my search budget ran out before I could check that point. I therefore mark it as possibly unexplored, with low confidence.
